sharedText: which was called the land of
reason: Six words of place-naming boilerplate. Deuteronomy's 'all the region of Argob, with all Bashan, which was called the land of giants' shares nothing with Alma's land of Mormon but the naming formula, which the Book of Mormon uses constantly. Covered in kind by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

sharedText: behold they were in the midst of
reason: A seven-word run built entirely from 'behold', 'they were' and 'in the midst of'. Elisha's servants find themselves in the middle of Samaria; Alma's fathers are in the midst of darkness. The verse does have a source — Ephesians 5:14, filed as a link — and the run is an accident of two common phrases meeting.

A near miss worth recording because the count looks decisive and is not. 'Chains of hell' is the engine of Alma 5:7-10, repeated four times, and it occurs in no KJV verse; the KJV's nearest phrases are 2 Peter 2:4's 'chains of darkness' (a singleton) and Jude 1:6's 'everlasting chains under darkness'. But in both of those the chained are angels, the chaining is permanent, and the purpose is to reserve them unto judgment — whereas Alma's chains are on human beings and the whole point of the passage is that they were loosed. The Book of Mormon has coined its phrase against the KJV's, not from it; 'bands of death' likewise occurs in no KJV verse. No source identifiable.

Isaiah 63:1-3's treader of the winepress, whose 'blood shall be sprinkled upon my garments', and Revelation 19:13's 'vesture dipped in blood' are the KJV's two bloodstained garments, and both are tempting in a passage that has just washed garments in blood at 5:21. Neither will do: in both the blood is the blood of enemies and the stained one is a conqueror, whereas Alma 5:22-23's stains testify that the wearer is a murderer. The verse's real source is the same as 5:21's, Revelation 7:14, used in reverse.

Mis-ranked in the dossier and formulaic in any case: 'the holy spirit of God' is the Book of Mormon's standing designation, used at 5:46 and 5:54 among many, and Ephesians 4:30's 'grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption' shares no other word with any of them.

sharedText: and now I say unto you
reason: The single commonest connective in this chapter, which uses 'I say unto you' more than forty times as the hinge of a rhetorical question. Ranked at 5:47, 5:57 and 5:59 alike. Gamaliel's counsel to the Sanhedrin has nothing else in common with any of them. One entry covers every occurrence in the chapter.

Ranked at 5:52 and again at 5:53, and genuinely apt in theme — Isaiah 10:33's high ones of stature hewn down and the haughty humbled would suit a sermon against pride. But the chapter's tree, axe, fruit and fire are Matthew 3:10 and 3:12 entire, and the passive 'shall be hewn down and cast into the fire' is that sentence's, not Isaiah's, which has no fire and no fruit. The link is filed at 5:52 to Matthew 3:10; Matthew 7:19 is kept there as a composite because it supplies the relative pronoun.

sharedText: turning your backs upon the poor, and the needy
reason: The same charge, in almost the same words, as Alma 4:12 — 'turning their backs upon the needy, and the naked' — where it is adjudicated against Matthew 25:44's roll of the neglected. Alma 5:55 is Alma quoting his own indictment back at the congregation he made it about, which is the sermon's method throughout this section (compare 5:53's costly apparel against 4:6). A reader arriving at 5:55 should be sent to Alma 4:12; nothing is added here that the earlier row does not carry.

sharedText: setting your hearts upon the vain things of the world, upon your riches
reason: Adjudicated at Alma 4:8, where the same clause — riches, vanity, and the setting of the heart — is argued against Psalm 62:9-10 and its KJV singleton 'set not your heart upon'. Alma 5:53 repeats it verbatim as part of the sermon's roll-call of the previous chapter's charges. The link at this verse is to Hebrews 10:29, for 'trample the holy one under your feet'; the riches clause belongs to 4:8.

A good example of a string match whose sense is exactly inverted. Jeremiah 17:13's 'they that depart from me shall be written in the earth' is a curse — to be written in dust is to be erased — and Alma 5:58's 'the names of the righteous shall be written in the Book of Life' is the blessing. The two verses use the same four words to say opposite things about the same people. The link at 5:57-58 is to Psalm 69:28, which has both halves of the Book of Mormon's antithesis in one verse.

Five words of promissory syntax. Deuteronomy 1:39 gives the land to the children who had no knowledge of good and evil; Alma 5:58 grants an inheritance at the right hand. The inheritance-at-the-right-hand image is Matthew 25:33-34's and is recorded in the recurrence of the link at 5:16.

sharedText: shepherds that do not feed the flock
reason: Ezekiel 34 is the Old Testament's long arraignment of shepherds who feed themselves and not the flock, and it is the passage a reader expecting a source for Alma 5:59's rhetorical question will reach for first. It will not bear the weight: Ezekiel's shepherds are the rulers of Israel and his complaint is that they have not sought the strayed, whereas Alma's question is about a shepherd who does his job — 'what shepherd is there among you having many sheep, doth not watch over them?' — and the wolf that answers it is not in Ezekiel 34 at all but in Acts 20:29 and John 10:12, where the link is filed. Ezekiel 34:11-16 does stand behind the Book of Mormon's shepherd language generally and is worth a reader's attention; it is not the source here.
